p: The dynasty, also called Temenid, had King Caranus as its mythical founder. Herodotus tells in The Histories that three brothers of the lineage of Temenus, named Gauanes, Aeropus and Perdiccas, fled from Argos to the Illyrians and then to a town called Lebaea in Upper Macedonia, where they served the king. Dismissed by him because of an omen that something great would happen to Perdiccas, they settled near the garden of Midas below Mount Bermio and slowly formed a kingdom of their own. A Greek inscription relating to the belief in descent from Heracles was found by Manolis Andronikos in the royal palace of Aigai, near modern Vergina.

According to Thucydides, in the History of the Peloponnesian War, the Argeads came down from the highlands to Lower Macedonia, expelled the Pierians from Pieria, gained a narrow strip along the river Axios reaching to Pella and the sea, and added Mygdonia by driving out the Edoni, Eordians and Almopians. Another theory, held by the Greek historian Miltiades Hatzopoulos following the ancient author Appian, is that the dynasty came from Argos Orestikon rather than from the Peloponnese, its people completing their wandering from Orestis to Lower Macedonia in the 7th century BCE.

The Argeads were at first rulers of the tribe of the same name, which prevailed in early Emathia, later Lower Macedonia, with its capital at Aigai. Herodotus relates that when Alexander I of Macedon entered the Olympic Games, in 504 or 500 BCE, other competitors objected that he was not Greek; the judges, the Hellanodikai, examined his Argead claim and allowed him to take part. By the time of Philip II of Macedon the kingdom, now governed from Pella, included all the states of Upper Macedonia.

The death of a king almost invariably set off disputes among members of the family, and often a war of succession. A six-year interregnum from 399 to 393 BCE followed the death of King Archelaus, and wars of succession followed the deaths of Pausanias, Amyntas III and Perdiccas III, the last of which brought Philip II to power in 360 to 359 BCE after he deposed Amyntas IV. An established king could also face rebellion by a relative, as Perdiccas II did from his brother Philip. Modern historians disagree on a number of details of the family's genealogy.

notes: Two sections: the saved article has only the origin legends and a list of succession disputes; its list of rulers and family tree are empty in the file.
The article gives the dynasty's end as 'c. 310 BC or 304 BC'; I did not restate an end date.
The article's long passage on Hatzopoulos's and Helly's dialect hypotheses was left out as it concerns the Macedonian language rather than the dynasty.
